Below is an overview of major classes of sedative agents, representative compounds, their typical legal status (U.S.-centric, noting that specifics vary by country), and common therapeutic uses. Wherever helpful, alternatives (OTC or “natural”) are also noted.

1. GABA­A–Receptor Positive Allosteric Modulators  
  a. Barbiturates  
    • Examples & scheduling (U.S.):  
      – Thiopental: not CSA-scheduled (hospital use only)  
      – Phenobarbital: Schedule IV  
      – Secobarbital, pentobarbital: Schedule II  
    • Mechanism: prolong GABA-mediated Cl– influx  
    • Therapeutic uses: anesthesia induction (thiopental), seizure prophylaxis/status epilepticus (phenobarbital), euthanasia (pentobarbital)  
    • Risks: narrow therapeutic index, tolerance, physical dependence, abuse potential (esp. secobarbital/pentobarbital)  

  b. Benzodiazepines  
    • All are Schedule IV (U.S.)  
    • Representative agents: diazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, midazolam  
    • Mechanism: increase frequency of GABA-gated Cl– channel opening  
    • Therapeutic uses: anxiety disorders, insomnia, alcohol‐withdrawal, procedural sedation, status epilepticus (lorazepam), muscle spasm  

  c. “Z-Drugs” (Non-BZD sedative-hypnotics)  
    • Zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone: Schedule IV  
    • Mechanism: selective α1-subunit GABA­A modulators  
    • Uses: short-term insomnia management  
    • Advantage: fewer muscle-relaxant/anticonvulsant effects than BZDs; still risk of tolerance, parasomnias  

2. General Anesthetics & Dissociatives  
  a. Intravenous agents  
    • Propofol: not CSA-scheduled; strictly hospital/research use  
    • Etomidate, ketamine (Schedule III), dexmedetomidine (prescription only, not CSA)  
    • Uses: induction/maintenance of general anesthesia; ketamine also for refractory depression/analgesia; dexmedetomidine for ICU sedation (α2-agonism)  

  b. Inhalational agents (all un-scheduled federally but restricted to clinical settings)  
    • Halogenated ethers: isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane  
    • Nitrous oxide (Schedule III in some U.S. states)  
    • Uses: operating-room anesthesia; nitrous oxide also analgesic in dentistry, obstetrics  

3. Antihistamines & Anticholinergics  
  a. First-generation H1 antagonists (OTC in many countries)  
    • Diphenhydramine, doxylamine  
    • Mechanism: central H1 blockade + anticholinergic effects  
    • Uses: OTC sleep aids; adjunct in pruritus, motion sickness  
    • Risks: daytime sedation, cognitive impairment, anticholinergic side effects  

4. Certain Antidepressants & Antipsychotics (off-label hypnotic use)  
  a. Trazodone (prescription; not scheduled)  
    • Low-dose sedation via 5-HT2A antagonism and H1 blockade  
    • Widely used off-label for insomnia  
  b. Mirtazapine (Rx; not scheduled)  
    • α2-antagonist and H1 blockade → sedation, appetite stimulation  
  c. Low-dose sedating antipsychotics (e.g., quetiapine)  
    • Used off-label for insomnia; caution regarding metabolic risks, off-target side effects  

5. Gabapentinoids & Muscle Relaxants  
  a. Pregabalin (Schedule V), gabapentin (unscheduled federally, but regulated in some states)  
    • Mechanism: α2δ subunit of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels  
    • Uses: neuropathic pain, generalized anxiety disorder (pregabalin), off-label insomnia/anxiolysis  
  b. Baclofen (Rx; not scheduled)  
    • GABA­B agonist → muscle relaxation, mild sedation  

6. “Natural” & Nutraceutical Sedatives  
  a. Melatonin (OTC dietary supplement)  
    • Regulation: unregulated by FDA as a drug  
    • Uses: circadian rhythm disorders, jet lag  
  b. Herbal extracts (OTC; quality varies)  
    • Valerian, passionflower, kava kava (restricted in some countries over hepatotoxicity concerns)  
    • Generally mild sedative effect; limited high-quality clinical data  

Therapeutic Applications by Setting  
  • Anxiety disorders & panic: benzodiazepines, pregabalin, buspirone (non-sedating anxiolytic)  
  • Insomnia: BZDs, Z-drugs, low-dose trazodone/mirtazapine, OTC antihistamines, melatonin  
  • Procedural/operative sedation: midazolam, propofol, etomidate, dexmedetomidine, inhalational agents  
  • ICU sedation: propofol, dexmedetomidine, midazolam infusion  
  • Seizure emergencies: IV lorazepam, diazepam, phenobarbital  
  • Alcohol-withdrawal: benzodiazepines, phenobarbital protocols  

Key Points on Legal Status & Control  
  – Controlled-substance scheduling reflects abuse potential, dependence risk, medical value.  
  – Prescription vs OTC varies: e.g. diphenhydramine is OTC, whereas most benzodiazepines require DEA-controlled prescriptions.  
  – Hospital-only agents (propofol, inhalational anesthetics) are tightly regulated but not CSA-scheduled.  
  – Nutraceuticals and many antidepressants/antipsychotics are prescription-only but generally not scheduled.  

When considering any sedative for research or clinical use, factors include pharmacokinetics (onset/duration), safety margin, dependence liability, comorbid medical conditions, and regulatory requirements in your jurisdiction.
